Global L∞L^{\infty}-bounds and long-time behavior of a diffusive epidemic system in heterogeneous environment Thanks: Submitted to the editors DATE.

Rui Peng ††thanks: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Jiangsu Normal University Xuzhou, 221116, Jiangsu, China (). Email: pengrui_seu@163.com    Yixiang Wu ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Vanderbilt University Nashville, TN 37212, USA (). Email: yixiang.wu@vanderbilt.edu
Abstract

In this paper, we are concerned with an epidemic reaction-diffusion system with nonlinear incidence mechanism of the form Sq​Ip​(p,q>0)S^{q}I^{p}\,(p,\,q>0). The coefficients of the system are spatially heterogeneous and time dependent (particularly time periodic). We first establish the L∞L^{\infty}-bounds of the solutions of a class of systems, which improve some previous results in [58]. Based on such estimates, we then study the long-time behavior of the solutions of the system. Our results reveal the delicate effect of the infection mechanism, transmission rate, recovery rate and disease-induced mortality rate on the infection dynamics. Our analysis can be adapted to models with some other types of infection incidence mechanisms.

keywords
Epidemic reaction-diffusion system; heterogeneous environment; nonlinear incidence mechanism; L∞L^{\infty}-bounds; long-time behavior.

1 Introduction

Transmission mechanisms play an essential role in susceptible-infected/host-pathogen/host-vector epidemic models [5, 50]. In the pioneering work of Kermack and McKendrick [29], the disease transmission was assumed to be governed via the mass action mechanism: the number of newly infected individuals per unit area per unit of time are given by a bilinear incidence function β​S​I\beta SI, where S,IS,\,I are the densities of susceptible and infected individuals, respectively, and β>0\beta>0 is the disease transmission rate. Nevertheless, as pointed out in several works including [14, 22, 50], such a bilinear incidence function carries some shortcomings and may require modifications in certain situations. As such, many different nonlinear incidence functions have been proposed to describe the transmission of infectious diseases. One commonly used nonlinear incidence function takes the form β​Sq​Ip\beta S^{q}I^{p}, where p,q>0p,\,q>0 are constants. Epidemic models with this incidence function have been studied extensively; one may refer to [23, 24, 25, 40, 42, 43, 44] and the references therein.

On the other hand, it has been recognized that environmental heterogeneity and individual motility are significant factors that should be taken into consideration when studying the spread and control of infectious diseases; one may refer to, for instance, [15, 48, 60] for relevant discussions. Many reaction-diffusion epidemic models have been developed to investigate the impact of them on the dynamics of disease transmissions, such as malaria [45, 46], rabies [27, 28, 53], dengue fever [61], West Nile virus [35, 62], hantavirus [1, 2], Asian longhorned beetle [20, 21], etc. These models are derived from the ordinary differential equation (ODE) compartmental epidemic models by introducing random diffusion terms to describe the movement of individuals and the spatiotemporally dependent coefficients to describe the environmental heterogeneity.

Taking into account spatial diffusion, environmental heterogeneity as well as a nonlinear incidence mechanism, we consider the following reaction-diffusion SI/SIS (S: susceptible, I: infected) epidemic system, which is a natural extension of the ODE epidemic models proposed by Kermack and McKendrick in [29, 30, 31, 32]:

{∂tS−dS​Δ​S=−β⁡(x,t)​Sq​Ip+γ⁡(x,t)​I,x∈Ω,t>0,∂tI−dI​Δ​I=β⁡(x,t)​Sq​Ip−[γ⁡(x,t)+μ⁡(x,t)]​I,x∈Ω,t>0,∂νS=∂νI=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,S(x,0)=S0(x),I(x,0)=I0(x),x∈Ω.\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}{\partial_{t}}S-d_{S}\Delta S=-\beta(x,t)S^{q}I^{p}+\gamma(x,t)I,&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ {\partial_{t}}I-d_{I}\Delta I=\beta(x,t)S^{q}I^{p}-[\gamma(x,t)+\mu(x,t)]I,&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ {\partial_{\nu}}S={\partial_{\nu}}I=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\,t>0,\\ S(x,0)=S_{0}(x),\,I(x,0)=I_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega.\\ \end{array}\right. (1)

Here, S⁡(x,t)S(x,t) and I⁡(x,t)I(x,t) are the density of susceptible and infected individuals at position xx and time tt, respectively; the habitat Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is a bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega; ν\nu is the unit outward normal of ∂Ω\partial\Omega and the homogeneous Neumann boundary condition means that there is no population flux across the boundary; dSd_{S} and dId_{I} are positive constants measuring the motility of susceptible and infected individuals, respectively; p,q>0p,\,q>0 are constants; β\beta is the disease transmission rate; γ\gamma is the disease recovery rate and μ\mu is the disease-induced death rate. If γ=0\gamma=0, (1) is an SI model; if γ≠0\gamma\neq 0, it is an SIS model.

The global dynamics of (1) with mass action incidence mechanism (i.e., p=q=1p=q=1) have been investigated by several researchers [13, 19, 36, 38, 64, 65, 66]. In [64], Webb studied the case that β\beta and μ\mu are positive constants and γ=0\gamma=0, and proved that SS converges to a positive number while II decays to zero; among other things, Li and Yip [36] derived the same result using a different approach. In [19], Fitzgibbon et al., obtained the same asymptotic result with β\beta and γ\gamma being spatially dependent. When μ=0\mu=0 and β,γ>0\beta,\,\gamma>0 are spatially dependent, (1) is an SIS epidemic model which was studied by [13, 65, 66]. In [38], Li et al. introduced a linear source term to the first equation of (1) to describe the demographic structure of the population. On the other hand, models related to (1) have been investigated, for instance, in [11, 12, 13, 34, 38, 37, 39, 54, 55, 56, 57]. These works were mostly motivated by [4], where Allen et al. considered (1) with standard incidence mechanism S​I/(S+I)SI/(S+I) and spatially dependent coefficients.

Model (1) belongs to a class of reaction-diffusion equations that has been studied extensively. Adding up the first two equations in (1) and integrating over Ω\Omega, we find

dd​t∫Ω(S(x,t)+I(x,t))dx=−∫ΩμI(x,t)dx,\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}(S(x,t)+I(x,t))dx=-\int_{\Omega}\mu I(x,t)dx, (2)

and therefore

∫Ω(S⁡(x,t)+I⁡(x,t))​𝑑x≤∫Ω(S0​(x)+I0​(x))​𝑑x:=N,t≥0,\int_{\Omega}(S(x,t)+I(x,t))dx\leq\int_{\Omega}(S_{0}(x)+I_{0}(x))dx:=N,\ \ t\geq 0, (3)

which means that the total population is bounded by NN. Models with such a property are called reaction-diffusion systems with control of mass, which are of the form:

{∂tu−d1​Δ​u=f⁡(u,v),x∈Ω,t>0,∂tv−d2​Δ​v=g⁡(u,v),x∈Ω,t>0,∂νu=∂νv=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x)≥0,v(x,0)=v0(x)≥0,x∈Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}{\partial_{t}}u-d_{1}\Delta u=f(u,v),&x\in{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\Omega},t>0,\\ {\partial_{t}}v-d_{2}\Delta v=g(u,v),&x\in{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\Omega},t>0,\\ {\partial_{\nu}}u={\partial_{\nu}}v=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0,\ \ v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0,&x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right. (4)

where f,g∈C1​(ℝ+2)f,g\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{2}) satisfies

  1. (P)

    f⁡(0,v)≥0​ and ​g​(u,0)≥0,∀u,v≥0f(0,v)\geq 0\ \text{ and }\ g(u,0)\geq 0,\ \ \forall u,\,v\geq 0,

and

  1. (M)

    f⁡(u,v)+g⁡(u,v)≤C⁡(1+u+v),∀u,v≥0f(u,v)+g(u,v)\leq C(1+u+v),\ \ \forall u,\,v\geq 0,

where CC is some nonnegative number.

In [58], (P) is called as the quasi-positive condition and (M) is the mass-control condition. When f=−u​vpf=-uv^{p} and g=u​vpg=uv^{p}, Alikakos [3] proved the global existence and L∞L^{\infty} boundedness of the solutions using the Alikakos-Moser iteration technique for the case 1≤p<(n+2)/n1\leq p<(n+2)/n. In [49], Masuda dropped the assumption on pp using a Lyapunov functional method. Moreover, Masuda proved the convergence of the solutions to nonnegative constants. When f=−uq​vp+us​vrf=-u^{q}v^{p}+u^{s}v^{r} and g=us​vr−uq​vpg=u^{s}v^{r}-u^{q}v^{p}, the system was studied in [33, 58]. For general functions ff and gg satisfying (P) and (M), Hollis et al. [26] studied the L∞L^{\infty} boundedness of the solutions, where a prior L∞L^{\infty}-bound on uu was assumed. In [51, 52], Morgan studied a more general reaction-diffusion system with control in mass, where the boundedness results were based on a Lyapunov-type condition on the nonlinearities. We refer the interested readers to the survey paper by Pierre [58] for more studies along this direction.

A priori L∞L^{\infty}-estimates are crucial in the study of the long-time behavior of the solutions of (1). System (4) admits a priori L1L^{1}-estimates, namely, (3). However, it is a rather challenging problem to bootstrap a priori L1L^{1}-estimates to L∞L^{\infty}-estimates. Indeed, concrete examples for (4) have been found that a priori L1L^{1}-estimates may lead to blow-up at finite time in the L∞L^{\infty}-norm; see [58, 59] and the references therein. Thus, in order to bootstrap L1L^{1}-estimates to L∞L^{\infty}-estimates, one has to impose extra conditions on the reaction terms. In this paper, we will show that the solutions of (1) are L∞L^{\infty}-bounded for all p,q>0p,q>0 and (1) is dissipative (i.e., solutions are ultimately uniformly L∞L^{\infty}-bounded).

With our L∞L^{\infty}-estimates, we can investigate the long-time behavior of the solutions of system (1). In the case μ>0\mu>0, we prove that the II-component of the solution decays to zero, while the SS-component of the solution converges to some nonnegative constant S∗S^{*}. More importantly, we show that S∗S^{*} is positive if p≥1p\geq 1 and S∗=0S^{*}=0 if 0<p<10<p<1. In the case μ=0\mu=0, we prove that (1) is uniformly persistent under certain conditions. We point out that one of the main difficulties of the analysis comes from the fact that Sq​IpS^{q}I^{p} is not Lipschitz when 0<p,q<10<p,q<1; for example, the solutions of (1) may not induce a semiflow on a complete metric space, and therefore many existing theories on dynamical systems cannot apply directly. We remark that the case 0<p<10<p<1 is important, which is the main consideration in [17, 40].

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we state the main results; in Section 3, we derive the L∞L^{\infty}-bounds of the solutions of a class of reaction-diffusion systems with control of mass; in Section 4, we prove the positivity, uniqueness and L∞L^{\infty}-boundedness of the solutions of (1); in Sections 5 and 6, we investigate the long-time behavior of the solutions; in Section 7, we discuss some possible generalizations and the biological implications of our results; in the appendix, we provide some helpful results on the ODE epidemic systems, which are usually the guidance for the analysis of the corresponding reaction-diffusion epidemic systems, and we state and generalize some results on dynamical systems defined on incomplete metric spaces, which are used in the proofs in Section 6.

2 Preliminaries and main results

2.1 Global existence and L∞L^{\infty}-bounds of (4)

We first recall some results about the global existence of the solutions of (4). In the survey paper [58], Pierre established the following result:

Proposition 2.1 ([58, Theorem 3.1]).

Suppose that (P)-(M), and the following hold:

f⁡(u,v)≤C⁡(1+u+v),|g⁡(u,v)|≤C⁡(1+ua+va),f(u,v)\leq C(1+u+v),\ \ |g(u,v)|\leq C(1+u^{a}+v^{a}),

for all u≥U,v≥0u\geq U,v\geq 0, where the constants U,C≥0,a>0U,C\geq 0,\,a>0. Then, for any nonnegative initial data u0,v0∈C⁡(Ω¯)u_{0},v_{0}\in C(\bar{\Omega}), the classical solution of (4) is nonnegative and exists globally.

In [58], the author applied Proposition 2.1 to system (4) with f=−uq​vp+λ​us​vrf=-u^{q}v^{p}+\lambda u^{s}v^{r}, g=us​vr−uq​vpg=u^{s}v^{r}-u^{q}v^{p} and λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], and derived sufficient conditions for the global existence of solutions. More precisely, for any nonnegative initial data u0,v0∈C⁡(Ω¯)u_{0},v_{0}\in C(\bar{\Omega}), the system has a unique nonnegative global classical solution if

p,q,r,s≥1p,\,q,\,r,\,s\geq 1 (5)

and one of (i)-(iv) in the following holds:

  1. (H1)

    (i) p>r≥0p>r\geq 0 and s​p−r​q≤p−rsp-rq\leq p-r; (ii) p=r≥0p=r\geq 0 and 0≤s<q0\leq s<q;
    (iii) s>q≥0s>q\geq 0 and s​p−r​q≤s−qsp-rq\leq s-q; (iv) s=q≥0s=q\geq 0 and 0≤p<r0\leq p<r.

Proposition 2.2 ([58, Theorem 3.1]).

Assume that (5) and one of (i)-(iv) in (H1) hold. Then, for any nonnegative initial data u0,v0∈C⁡(Ω¯)u_{0},v_{0}\in C(\bar{\Omega}), system (4) with f=−uq​vp+λ​us​vrf=-u^{q}v^{p}+\lambda u^{s}v^{r}, g=us​vr−uq​vpg=u^{s}v^{r}-u^{q}v^{p} for λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] admits a unique nonnegative global classical solution.

To include (1) and (4) with f=−uq​vp+λ​us​vr,g=us​vr−uq​vpf=-u^{q}v^{p}+\lambda u^{s}v^{r},g=u^{s}v^{r}-u^{q}v^{p}, we consider the following system:

{∂tu−du​Δ​u=−β​uq​vp+γ​us​vr,x∈Ω,t>0,∂tv−dv​Δ​v=β​uq​vp−[γ+μ]​us​vr,x∈Ω,t>0,∂νu=∂νv=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x),v(x,0)=v0(x),x∈Ω,\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}\displaystyle{{\partial_{t}u}}-d_{u}\Delta u=-\beta u^{q}v^{p}+\gamma u^{s}v^{r},&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{{\partial_{t}v}}-d_{v}\Delta v=\beta u^{q}v^{p}-[\gamma+\mu]u^{s}v^{r},&x\in\Omega,\,t>0,\\ \displaystyle{\partial_{\nu}u}=\displaystyle{\partial_{\nu}v}=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\,t>0,\\ \displaystyle u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\,v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right. (6)

where p,q,s,rp,q,s,r are nonnegative constants and u0,v0∈C⁡(Ω¯)u_{0},v_{0}\in C(\bar{\Omega}) are nonnegative. The coefficients β\beta, γ\gamma and μ\mu are assumed to be nonnegative constants temporarily as they do not play an essential role in establishing the boundedness results here.

The results in [58] require condition (5). In this paper, we will show that, without condition (5), once the solution of system (6) exists globally, it must be uniformly bounded and the system is dissipative provided that either case in (H1) holds. Moreover, we are able to obtain some different parameter ranges which ensure the uniform boundedness of solution; that is, we will deal with the following parameter ranges:

  1. (H2)

    (i) 0≤p<10\leq p<1, 0≤s<q0\leq s<q, p​s−q​r≥s−qps-qr\geq s-q;
    (ii) 0≤s<10\leq s<1, 0≤p<r0\leq p<r, p​s−q​r≥p−rps-qr\geq p-r.

Throughout this paper, NN is the initial total mass, i.e. for system (4)

N=∫Ω(u0​(x)+v0​(x))​𝑑x,N=\int_{\Omega}(u_{0}(x)+v_{0}(x))dx,

while NN is given by (3) for system (1).

Our L∞L^{\infty}-boundedness results on (6) can be stated as follows.

Theorem 2.1.

Suppose that β>0\beta>0, γ,μ≥0\gamma,\mu\geq 0, and one of (H1)-(i), (H1)-(ii) or (H2)-(i) holds. Let (u,v)(u,v) be a nonnegative classical solution of (6). Then there exists M∞>0M_{\infty}>0 depending on the initial data such that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω),‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤M∞,∀t≥0.\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\ \ \|v(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq M_{\infty},\ \forall t\geq 0. (7)

Suppose in addition that p=r=1p=r=1 when (H1)-(ii) holds. Then, there exists N∞N_{\infty} depending only on NN such that, for any global classical solution (u,v)(u,v), the following hold:

lim supt→∞‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω),lim supt→∞‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤N∞.\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\ \ \limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq N_{\infty}. (8)

Remark 2.1.

Eq. (8) means that the system is dissipative, which is essential for proving the uniform persistence of (1) later on. If (5) is true, then (7) assures that a local solution can be uniquely extended to be a global solution. If (5) is not assumed, the solution may fail to be unique since uq​vpu^{q}v^{p} or us​vru^{s}v^{r} may not be Lipschitz.

In the case that one of (H1)-(iii), (H1)-(iv) or (H2)-(ii) holds, we can also establish the uniform boundedness result just by exchanging the roles of uu and vv in our analysis of Section 3 below.

Theorem 2.2.

Suppose that β≥0\beta\geq 0, γ+μ>0\gamma+\mu>0, and one of (H1)-(iii), (H1)-(iv) or (H2)-(ii) holds. Let (u,v)(u,v) be the a nonnegative classical solution of (6). Then there exists M∞>0M_{\infty}>0 depending on the initial data such that (7) holds. Suppose in addition that q=s=1q=s=1 when (H1)-(iv) holds. Then, there exists N∞N_{\infty} depending only on NN such that (8) holds for any global classical solution (u,v)(u,v).

2.2 Global existence, positivity, L∞L^{\infty}-bounds and dissipativity of (1)

We now turn to system (1) and let the coefficients β⁡(x,t),γ⁡(x,t),μ⁡(x,t)\beta(x,t),\gamma(x,t),\mu(x,t) be dependent on xx and tt. We impose the following assumptions for (1):

  1. (A1)

    The functions β,γ,μ\beta,\gamma,\mu are Hölder continuous with

    0≤β⁡(x,t),γ⁡(x,t),μ⁡(x,t)≤σ0on​Ω¯×[0,∞),0\leq\beta(x,t),\ \gamma(x,t),\ \mu(x,t)\leq\sigma^{0}\ \ \mbox{on}\ \bar{\Omega}\times[0,\infty),

    and, there exists some constant σ0>0\sigma_{0}>0 such that β⁡(x,t)>σ0\beta(x,t)>\sigma_{0} for all x∈Ω¯x\in\bar{\Omega} and t>0t>0.

  2. (A2)

    S0S_{0} and I0I_{0} are nonnegative continuous functions on Ω¯\bar{\Omega}. Moreover,

    1. (i)

      The initial value I0≥,≢0I_{0}\geq,\not\equiv 0 on Ω¯\bar{\Omega};

    2. (ii)

      If 0<q<10<q<1, S0​(x)>0S_{0}(x)>0 for all x∈Ω¯x\in\bar{\Omega}, and there exists σ0>0\sigma_{0}>0 such that γ≥σ0\gamma\geq\sigma_{0} for all x∈Ω¯x\in\bar{\Omega} and t≥0t\geq 0;

    3. (iii)

      If 0<p<10<p<1, I0​(x)>0I_{0}(x)>0 for all x∈Ω¯x\in\bar{\Omega}.

Remark 2.2.

Biologically, (A1) means that the disease transmission, recovery and mortality rates are bounded and nonnegative. (A2) is imposed to guarantee the global existence and the positivity of the solutions of (1):

  • •

    If I0=0I_{0}=0, then the component I⁡(x,t)=0I(x,t)=0 for all x∈Ω¯,t≥0x\in\bar{\Omega},\,t\geq 0, which is not of our interests.

  • •

    If γ=0\gamma=0 and 0<q<10<q<1, it is possible for S⁡(x,t)S(x,t) to vanish at some finite time; see Proposition 9.1-(i) in the appendix.

  • •

    When either 0<p<10<p<1 or 0<q<10<q<1, the term Sq​IpS^{q}I^{p} is not locally Lipschitz unless S,I>0S,I>0. Therefore, we have to assume the positivity of the initial data to ensure the uniqueness of the local solution. Moreover, the unique extension of the local solution requires the positivity of the solution.

We have the following result on the global existence, positivity and L∞L^{\infty}-bounds of the solutions of (1).

Theorem 2.3.

Assume that (A1)-(A2) hold. Then system (1) has a unique global classical solution (S,I)(S,I) for any p,q>0p,q>0 with S⁡(x,t),I⁡(x,t)>0S(x,t),I(x,t)>0 for all x∈Ω¯x\in\bar{\Omega} and t>0t>0, and there exists M∞>0M_{\infty}>0 depending on the initial data such that

‖S⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω),‖I⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤M∞,t≥0.\|S(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\ \ \|I(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq M_{\infty},\ \ t\geq 0. (9)

Moreover, there exists N∞N_{\infty} depending only on NN such that

lim supt→∞‖S⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω),lim supt→∞‖I⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤N∞.\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|S(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},\ \ \limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|I(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq N_{\infty}. (10)

2.3 Long-time behavior of (1)

In this section, we state our results on the long-time behavior of the solutions of (1).

(a) Case μ>0\mu>0 on Ω¯×[0,∞)\bar{\Omega}\times[0,\infty)

In this case, we further assume that

  • (A3)

    There exists σ0>0\sigma_{0}>0 such that μ⁡(x,t)≥σ0\mu(x,t)\geq\sigma_{0} for all x∈Ω¯x\in\bar{\Omega} and t≥0t\geq 0.

Biologically, (A3) means that there are losses of infected individuals due to disease-induced mortality. Under (A3), our main result about the dynamical behavior of the solution of (1) reads as follows.

Theorem 2.4.

Assume that (A1)-(A3) hold. Let (S,I)(S,I) be the unique solution of (1). Then the following assertions hold:

  • (i)

    If p≥1p\geq 1, we have (S,I)→(S∗,0)(S,I)\to(S_{*},0) uniformly on Ω¯\bar{\Omega} as t→∞t\to\infty, where S∗S_{*} is a positive constant. Moreover, S∗∈(0,supΩ×(0,∞)(γ+μ)/β]S_{*}\in(0,\sup_{\Omega\times(0,\infty)}{(\gamma+\mu)}/{\beta}] if p=1p=1.

  • (ii)

    If 0<p<10<p<1, we have (S,I)→(0,0)(S,I)\to(0,0) uniformly on Ω¯\bar{\Omega} as t→∞t\to\infty.

(b) Case μ=0\mu=0 on Ω¯×[0,∞)\bar{\Omega}\times[0,\infty)

In this case, the disease is not fatal. We further assume that the coefficients are periodic in time, i.e.,

  1. (A4)

    The functions β\beta and γ\gamma are periodic with the common period ω>0\omega>0, i.e., β⁡(x,t+ω)=β⁡(x,t)\beta(x,t+\omega)=\beta(x,t) and γ⁡(x,t+ω)=γ⁡(x,t)\gamma(x,t+\omega)=\gamma(x,t) for all x∈Ω¯x\in\bar{\Omega} and t≥0t\geq 0.

Biologically, (A4) means that the epidemic is seasonal. We have the following result about the uniform persistence of the solutions and the existence of a positive ω\omega-periodic solution of (1). The definition of the basic reproduction number, ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0}, is given by (63).

Theorem 2.5 (Uniform persistence).

Let μ=0\mu=0. Assume that (A1)-(A2) and (A4) hold, and let 0<p≤10<p\leq 1. We further assume ℛ0>1\mathcal{R}_{0}>1 if p=1p=1. Then there exists ϵ0>0\epsilon_{0}>0 depending only on NN such that for any solution (S,I)(S,I) of (1), we have

lim inft→∞S⁡(x,t),lim inft→∞I⁡(x,t)≥ϵ0,\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}S(x,t),\ \ \liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}I(x,t)\geq\epsilon_{0}, (11)

uniformly for x∈Ω¯x\in\bar{\Omega}. Moreover, (1) has at least one positive ω\omega-periodic solution.

Remark 2.3.

We would like to make the following comments for Theorem 2.5.

  • (i)

    When p=1p=1, we suspect that if ℛ0>1\mathcal{R}_{0}>1, (1) admits a unique positive equilibrium which is globally attractive, whereas the unique disease-free (II-component is zero) equilibrium is globally attractive if ℛ0≤1\mathcal{R}_{0}\leq 1. One may follow the same analysis as in [13, Theorems 4.1, 4.2] to prove this for the special cases when either β,γ\beta,\,\gamma are positive constants or dS=dId_{S}=d_{I}.

  • (ii)

    When p>1p>1, Proposition 9.2 of the appendix analyzes the long-time behavior of the ODE version of (1) which suggests that the dynamics of (1) depends on the initial data.

4 Proof of Theorem 2.3

We first prove the following result about the local existence and positivity of the solutions of (1).

Lemma 4.1.

Assume that (A1)-(A2) hold. Then (1) has a unique solution (S,I)(S,I) on Ω¯×[0,Tm​a​x)\bar{\Omega}\times[0,T_{max}), where Tm​a​x≤∞T_{max}\leq\infty is the maximal time for the existence of solution. Moreover, (S,I)(S,I) satisfies

S⁡(x,t),I⁡(x,t)>0for all(x,t)∈Ω¯×(0,Tm​a​x),S(x,t),I(x,t)>0\ \ \text{for all}\ \ (x,t)\in\bar{\Omega}\times(0,T_{max}),

Lemma 6.1 (Uniform weak persistence).

Now we are ready to prove the uniform persistence of the solutions and the existence of a positive ω\omega-periodic solution of (59)-(60). The definitions and results from dynamical systems theory used below can be found in the appendix. Since the semiflow induced by the solutions of (59)-(60) is not defined on a complete metric space, small modifications are necessary.

Remark 6.1.
  • (i)

    If p=1,q≥1p=1,q\geq 1 and ℛ0>1\mathcal{R}_{0}>1, with the aid of Theorem 2.3, we just need to slightly modify the analysis of [57, Theorem 3.3] to prove the uniform persistence result (i.e., we do not need to prove the uniform weak persistence first).

  • (ii)

    When p=1p=1, the same argument of [13, Theorem 2.1] allows one to conclude that the solution of (59) is bounded by a positive constant which depends on the initial data; however, such estimates are insufficient for us to obtain Theorem 2.5.

7 Discussion

In this section, we first discuss further applications of our analysis used in this paper to some other epidemic models. Then we interpret the biological implications of our results and conclude the influence of the parameters and coefficients of the model on the dynamical behavior of disease transmissions.

7.1 Other related epidemic models

We want to mention that the mathematical techniques developed in the previous sections can be carried over to other types of infection incidence functions, including the following ones:

  • (i)

    The binomial incidence function S​ln⁡(1+k​I)S\ln(1+kI) with k≥0k\geq 0 ([6, 7, 50]);

  • (ii)

    The incidence function Sq​Ip1+Iℓ\frac{S^{q}I^{p}}{1+I^{\ell}} with constants p,q>0,ℓ≥0p,q>0,\,\ell\geq 0 ([14, 25, 42, 44]);

  • (iii)

    The media effect incidence function Sq​Ip1+Iℓ​e−I\frac{S^{q}I^{p}}{1+I^{\ell}}e^{-I} with constants p,q>0,ℓ≥0p,q>0,\,\ell\geq 0 ([9, 10]).

More precisely, if Sq​IpS^{q}I^{p} is replaced by S​ln⁡(1+k​I)S\ln(1+kI) in (1), we can prove the same results as in Theorems 2.3, 2.4 and 2.5 for p=1p=1; if Sq​IpS^{q}I^{p} is replaced by Sq​Ip1+Iℓ\frac{S^{q}I^{p}}{1+I^{\ell}} or Sq​Ip1+Iℓ​e−I\frac{S^{q}I^{p}}{1+I^{\ell}}e^{-I} in (1), we can prove the same results as in Theorems 2.3, 2.4 and 2.5.

7.2 Conclusion

Usually, a priori L∞L^{\infty}-bounds are the starting point to study the long-time behavior of the solutions of a reaction-diffusion system. In this paper, we establish the L∞L^{\infty}-bounds for (6) first. Our results include a range of parameters which are not covered by [18, 52, 58], and the technique developed in the proof of Theorem 2.1 under (H2) may find further applications in other reaction-diffusion systems. We remark that if p,q≥1p,q\geq 1 one may apply the results in [18, 52] to obtain the L∞L^{\infty}-bounds in Theorem 2.3 for (1) but not for (6) in general; if p<1p<1 or q<1q<1, the positivity of the solutions is required to ensure the unique extension of the solutions, and therefore the analysis is more subtle.

Based on the L∞L^{\infty}-bounds, we investigate the long-time behavior of the solutions of (1) in the following two cases:

(i) μ>0 and (ii) μ=0.\begin{array}[]{l}\mbox{(i)\ \, $\mu>0$ \ \ \ and\ \ \ (ii)\ \, $\mu=0$}.\end{array}

The global dynamics of (1) are very different for these two cases.

The case (i) states that there are individuals who die from the disease and thus the total population number of susceptible and infected hosts is decreasing in time tt as seen from (2). In this case, Theorem 2.4 shows that I⁡(x,t)I(x,t) converges to zero, which means that the infection will become extinct in the long run. However, the long-time behavior of S⁡(x,t)S(x,t) depends on the parameter pp:

  • •

    When p≥1p\geq 1, the density of susceptible individuals converges to a positive constant, which means that the susceptible population will distribute homogeneously in the whole habitat eventually;

  • •

    When 0<p<10<p<1, the density of susceptible individuals converges to zero which means that the disease is fatal enough so that it drives its hosts to extinction.

The case (ii) biologically means that the disease is not fatal. From (2) it follows that the total population of susceptible and infected remains constant all the time. According to Theorem 2.5 and Remark 2.3, we see that

  • •

    When 0<p<10<p<1 or p=1p=1 with the basic production number ℛ0>1\mathcal{R}_{0}>1, the susceptible and infected populations uniformly persist in the whole habitat in the long run;

  • •

    When p=1p=1 and ℛ0≤1\mathcal{R}_{0}\leq 1, the disease dies out and the susceptible population persists.

  • •

    When p>1p>1, Remark 2.3(ii) indicates that the dynamics of (59)-(60) will depend on the initial data and the susceptible population will not be driven to extinction.

The above discussion shows that in an SI/SIS system with nonlinear incidence function Sq​Ip​(p,q>0)S^{q}I^{p}\,(p,\,q>0), the power pp and the disease-induced death rate μ\mu are vital factors in determining the global dynamics; in particular, if the disease-induced death rate μ\mu is taken into account, the fatal disease causes its hosts to extinction if and only if 0<p<10<p<1.

It is further worth mentioning that in a very recent work [17], Farrell et al. studied a class of SI ODE systems in which the incidence function Sq​IpS^{q}I^{p} is one of the main focuses. In particular, they explored the roles of the exponents p,qp,q on the extinction of the susceptible population. One may refer to [17] and the references therein for more experimental observations and theoretical analysis regarding the phenomenon of host extinction caused by infectious diseases.

Since S⁡(t)+I⁡(t)=NS(t)+I(t)=N for all t≥0t\geq 0, it suffices to consider

{S′=−β​Sq​(N−S)p+γ⁡(N−S),t>0,S⁡(0)=S0∈(0,N).\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}{S^{\prime}}=-\beta S^{q}(N-S)^{p}+\gamma(N-S),&\,t>0,\\ \displaystyle S(0)=S_{0}\in(0,N).\end{array}\right. (83)

A standard phase plane analysis of (83) yields the desired results, and we omit the details here.

9.3 Some definitions and abstract results on dynamical systems

We collect the definitions and results on dynamical systems used in the current paper. These results can be found in [47, 67], however small modifications are needed since the map is not defined in a complete set in our applications.

Let (X,d)(X,d) be a complete metric space, and let ρ:X→[0,∞)\rho:X\rightarrow[0,\infty) be a continuous function. Define

X0:={x∈X:ρ⁡(x)>0}and∂X0:={x∈X:ρ⁡(x)=0}.X_{0}:=\{x\in X:\rho(x)>0\}\ \ \text{and}\ \ \partial X_{0}:=\{x\in X:\rho(x)=0\}.

For the maps defined on XX, we adopt all the definitions and terminology in [47, 67]. For (1), when 0<p<10<p<1 or 0<q<10<q<1, the solution may fail to be unique if the initial data are not strictly positive. Taking this into consideration, we consider a continuous map T:X0→X0T:X_{0}\rightarrow X_{0}.

For any two sets A,B⊂XA,B\subset X and x∈Ax\in A, we let

d⁡(x,A)=infy∈Ad⁡(x,y) and δ⁡(B,A)=supx∈Bd⁡(x,A).d(x,A)=\inf_{y\in A}d(x,y)\ \ \text{ and }\ \ \delta(B,A)=\sup_{x\in B}d(x,A).

We say that A⊂XA\subset X attracts B⊂X0B\subset X_{0} for TT if limn→∞δ⁡(Tn​(B),A)=0\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\delta(T^{n}(B),A)=0.

Definition 1.

A continuous map T:X0→X0T:X_{0}\rightarrow X_{0} is said to be compact if for any bounded set B⊂XB\subset X, T⁡(B∩X0)T(B\cap X_{0}) is precompact in XX; TT is point dissipative if there is a bounded set B⊂XB\subset X such that BB attracts each point in X0X_{0}; T is asymptotically smooth if for any closed bounded set B⊂XB\subset X with T⁡(B∩X0)⊂B∩X0T(B\cap X_{0})\subset B\cap X_{0}, there is a compact set J⊂BJ\subset B such that JJ attracts B∩X0B\cap X_{0}.

The following result is a variant of [47, Theorem 2.6 (a)].

Proposition 9.3.

Let T:X0→X0T:X_{0}\rightarrow X_{0} be a continuous map. Suppose that TT is point dissipative and asymptotically smooth. Then there is a compact set M⊂XM\subset X, which attracts each point in X0X_{0} for TT.

Proof.

Since TT is point dissipative, there exists a bounded set B⊂XB\subset X such that for any x∈X0x\in X_{0}, there exists N=N⁡(x)N=N(x), Tn​(x)∈B∩X0T^{n}(x)\in B\cap X_{0} for all n≥Nn\geq N. Let J⁡(B)J(B) be defined by

J(B)={y∈B∩X0:Tn(y)∈B∩X0,for alln≥0}.J(B)=\{y\in B\cap X_{0}:T^{n}(y)\in B\cap X_{0},\ \text{for all}\ n\geq 0\}.

Clearly, J⁡(B)J(B) is not empty. Indeed, for any x∈X0x\in X_{0}, we have Tn​(x)∈J​(B)T^{n}(x)\in J(B) for all n≥Nn\geq N. Since TT is continuous, J⁡(B)¯∩X0=J⁡(B)\overline{J(B)}\cap X_{0}=J(B). To see this, we first note J⁡(B)⊂J⁡(B)¯∩X0J(B)\subset\overline{J(B)}\cap X_{0} as J⁡(B)⊂X0J(B)\subset X_{0}. For any x∈J⁡(B)¯∩X0x\in\overline{J(B)}\cap X_{0}, there exists {xk}⊂J⁡(B)\{x_{k}\}\subset J(B) such that xk→xx_{k}\rightarrow x. For each k≥0k\geq 0, since xk∈J⁡(B)x_{k}\in J(B), Tn​(xk)∈B∩X0T^{n}(x_{k})\in B\cap X_{0} for all n≥0n\geq 0. By the continuity of TT, Tn​(x)∈B∩X0T^{n}(x)\in B\cap X_{0} for all n≥0n\geq 0. Therefore, x∈J⁡(B)x\in J(B) and J⁡(B)¯∩X0⊂J⁡(B)\overline{J(B)}\cap X_{0}\subset J(B).

Since J⁡(B)¯\overline{J(B)} is bounded with T⁡(J⁡(B)¯∩X0)=T⁡(J⁡(B))⊂J⁡(B)T(\overline{J(B)}\cap X_{0})=T(J(B))\subset J(B) and TT is asymptotically smooth, there exists a compact set M⊂XM\subset X such that MM attracts J⁡(B)J(B). It is not hard to check that MM attracts each point in X0X_{0}.

Definition 2.

Let T:X0→X0T:X_{0}\rightarrow X_{0} be a continuous map. TT is said to be ρ\rho-uniformly persistent if there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that lim infn→∞ρ⁡(Tn​(x))≥ϵ\liminf_{n\rightarrow\infty}\rho(T^{n}(x))\geq\epsilon for all x∈X0x\in X_{0}; TT is weakly ρ\rho-uniformly persistent if there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that lim supn→∞ρ⁡(Tn​(x))≥ϵ\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\rho(T^{n}(x))\geq\epsilon for all x∈X0x\in X_{0}.

The proof of the following result is exactly the same as [47, Proposition 3.2].

Proposition 9.4.

Let T:X0→X0T:X_{0}\rightarrow X_{0} be a continuous map. Suppose that there exists a compact set M⊂XM\subset X which attracts each point in X0X_{0} for TT. Then if TT is weakly ρ\rho-uniformly persistent, it is ρ\rho-uniformly persistent.

A bounded subset B⊂X0B\subset X_{0} is ρ\rho-strongly bounded if there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that infx∈Bρ⁡(x)>0\inf_{x\in B}\rho(x)>0. The following result is borrowed from [47, Theorem 3.8(a)] with slight modification.

Proposition 9.5.

Let XX and X0X_{0} be defined as above. Suppose in addition that XX is a closed subset of some Banach space with the metric dd induced by the norm and X0X_{0} is convex. Let T:X0→X0T:X_{0}\rightarrow X_{0} be a continuous map. Suppose that TT is compact, point dissipative, ρ\rho-uniformly persistent, and it maps ρ\rho-strongly bounded subsets of X0X_{0} to ρ\rho-strongly bounded subsets in X0X_{0}. Then TT has a fixed point in X0X_{0}.

Proof.

Let d0d_{0} be the metric on M0M_{0} as introduced in [47]:

d0​(x,y)=|1ρ⁡(x)−1ρ⁡(y)|+d⁡(x,y),x,y∈M0.d_{0}(x,y)=\left|\frac{1}{\rho(x)}-\frac{1}{\rho(y)}\right|+d(x,y),\ \ x,y\in M_{0}.

Then (M0,d0)(M_{0},d_{0}) is a complete metric space [47, Lemma 3.5]. Thus, all the terminology for T:(M0,d0)→(M0,d0)T:(M_{0},d_{0})\rightarrow(M_{0},d_{0}) (eg. global attractor, dissipativity, asymptotical smoothness) can be adopted in the usual sense. Moreover, for any subset B⊂X0B\subset X_{0}, BB is bounded in (X0,d0)(X_{0},d_{0}) if and only if it is ρ\rho-strongly bounded in (X0,d)(X_{0},d); if BB is closed (compact) in (X0,d)(X_{0},d), then it is closed (compact) in (X0,d0)(X_{0},d_{0}); if BB is closed (compact) and bounded in (X0,d0)(X_{0},d_{0}), then it is closed (compact) in (X0,d)(X_{0},d).

Since T:(X0,d)→(X0,d)T:(X_{0},d)\rightarrow(X_{0},d) is ρ\rho-uniformly persistent and point dissipative, T:(X0,d0)→(X0,d0)T:(X_{0},d_{0})\rightarrow(X_{0},d_{0}) is point dissipative. Since T:(X0,d)→(X0,d)T:(X_{0},d)\rightarrow(X_{0},d) is compact and TT maps ρ\rho-strongly bounded subsets of X0X_{0} to ρ\rho-strongly bounded subsets of X0X_{0}, then T:(X0,d0)→(X0,d0)T:(X_{0},d_{0})\rightarrow(X_{0},d_{0}) is compact. To see this, let B⊂X0B\subset X_{0} be bounded in (X0,d0)(X_{0},d_{0}), then it is ρ\rho-strongly bounded in (X0,d)(X_{0},d). Therefore, T⁡(B)T(B) is ρ\rho-strongly bounded in (X0,d)(X_{0},d) and T⁡(B)¯d\overline{T(B)}^{d} is compact in (X,d)(X,d). Since T⁡(B)T(B) is ρ\rho-strongly bounded, we have T⁡(B)¯d0=T⁡(B)¯d⊂X0\overline{T(B)}^{d_{0}}=\overline{T(B)}^{d}\subset X_{0}, which is compact in (X0,d0)(X_{0},d_{0}). Since T:(X0,d0)→(X0,d0)T:(X_{0},d_{0})\rightarrow(X_{0},d_{0}) is compact and point dissipative, it has a global attract A0⊂X0A_{0}\subset X_{0} ([67, Theorem 1.1.3]) and a fixed point x0∈A0x_{0}\in A_{0} ([67, Theorem 1.3.8]).
